newsitem.title: JAPAN: Dollar battered but off earlier lows by late Tokyo.
newsitem.headline: Dollar battered but off earlier lows by late Tokyo.

text.p: 0650 GMT TRADED HIGH/LOW AS OF 0600 GMT
The dollar was battered against the yen on Monday due to renewed concerns about Japan's trade surplus, briefly falling as low as 111.80 yen in midday trade, its lowest since November 25, 1996.
Comments by Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka calling for stability in currency rates helped lift the dollar from its lows, but it remained vulnerable to more losses, dealers said.

"The market is betting that Japan is trying to avoid criticism over its trade surplus at the (forthcoming Denver) summit by letting the yen drift higher," said Ryosuke Tsuji, senior vice president of forex at Societe Generale in Tokyo.

Given weak domestic demand in Japan, pushing the yen higher would be the only option for Japan to avoid an increase in its surplus with the United States. Dealers said the dollar is likely to fall to around 110 yen in the near term.
Economists said that Japan's current account surplus for April, due out on Wednesday, is expected to jump due to a decline in imports amid sluggish domestic demand.

Although dealers said fundamental factors still favour dollar buying despite weaker-than-expected U.S. May jobs data released on Friday, traders were shifting their attention to political issues ahead of the G7 summit.

"The Denver summit on June 20 and Japan's current account data on June 11 are seen as dollar-selling factors," a dealer at a European bank in Tokyo said. U.S. Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky voiced concerns on Friday over Japan's rising trade surplus with the United States.
Japanese trust banks, overseas funds and Japanese car makers were among sellers of the dollar, dealers said.
